claims.claim: Justin Martyr was born c. 100 at Flavia Neapolis (Nablus), studied with several philosophical schools, taught in Rome and was beheaded c. 165.
claims.source: Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 1–8; Martyrdom of Justin; Eusebius, Church History IV.16.

claims.claim: The First Apology was written c. 155 to Antoninus Pius; chapters 61, 65–67 describe baptism and the Sunday service.
claims.source: Justin, First Apology 1, 61, 65–67, tr. Dods and Reith, ANF I (1885), New Advent 0126.

claims.claim: Justin 66 is the earliest passage outside the New Testament to call the books about Jesus 'Gospels'.
claims.source: Standard claim: e.g. Graham Stanton, Jesus and Gospel (2004).

claims.claim: Acts 20:7 is the earliest clear mention of Christians gathering on the first day of the week to break bread; Paul at Troas c. AD 57.
claims.source: Acts 20:7–12; dating per standard Pauline chronology.

claims.claim: The Didache was found in 1873 in Constantinople (published by Bryennios 1883); usually dated c. 50–120, probably Syria.
claims.source: Aaron Milavec, The Didache (2003); Kurt Niederwimmer, The Didache (Hermeneia, 1998).

claims.claim: Pliny's letter (c. 112) reports a fixed day before dawn, a hymn to Christ 'as to a god', an oath, and a later harmless meal given up after his edict.
claims.source: Pliny, Letters X.96.

claims.claim: Ignatius, To the Magnesians 9, speaks of no longer sabbatising but living by the Lord's day (c. 110).
claims.source: Ignatius, Magnesians 9.

claims.claim: Constantine's law of 7 March 321 made Sunday a day of rest for courts and townspeople, allowing farm work.
claims.source: Codex Justinianus 3.12.2.

claims.claim: Easter controversy: Quartodecimans in Asia; Polycarp and Anicetus c. 155 parted in peace; Nicaea (325) fixed Easter on a Sunday.
claims.source: Eusebius, Church History V.23–24; Eusebius, Life of Constantine III.18.

claims.claim: Heschel called the Sabbath a 'palace in time' (1951).
claims.source: A. J. Heschel, The Sabbath (1951).

claims.claim: Dix's four actions (taken, thanked, broken, given) from the seven of the Last Supper.
claims.source: Gregory Dix, The Shape of the Liturgy (1945), ch. 4.

claims.claim: 'Liturgy' (leitourgia) in Athens meant a public service paid for by a citizen, e.g. a trireme or a chorus.
claims.source: Liddell–Scott–Jones s.v. leitourgia; Aristotle, Athenian Constitution 56.

claims.claim: Westminster Confession ch. 21 treats the Lord's day as the Christian Sabbath.
claims.source: Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), 21.7–8.

claims.claim: Jewish ritual immersion pools (mikvaot) of the first century have been found in large numbers, many around the Temple.
claims.source: Ronny Reich, studies of Jerusalem miqva'ot; E. P. Sanders, Jewish Law from Jesus to the Mishnah (1990).

claims.claim: Romans written c. 57 from Corinth; 1 Thessalonians c. 50; 1 Corinthians c. 54 from Ephesus; Matthew c. 70–90.
claims.source: Standard introductions, e.g. Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament (1997).

claims.claim: Augustine defined a sacrament as a visible sign of invisible grace; held baptism valid whoever gives it (against the Donatists).
claims.source: Augustine, City of God X.5; On Baptism against the Donatists; Tractates on John 80.3 ('visible word').

claims.claim: Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381) confesses 'one baptism for the remission of sins'.
claims.source: Creed of Constantinople, 381.

claims.claim: BEM (Lima 1982) asks churches to avoid anything that looks like rebaptism and calls infant and believer baptism equivalent alternatives.
claims.source: Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry, Baptism 13 and commentary 12.

claims.claim: Apostolic Tradition describes catechumenate up to three years and forbidden trades; date and authorship debated.
claims.source: Apostolic Tradition 15–17; Bradshaw, Johnson and Phillips, The Apostolic Tradition (Hermeneia, 2002).

claims.claim: Egeria (381–384) records the newly baptised applauding the bishop's explanations in Easter week.
claims.source: Egeria, Travels 47.

claims.claim: Dura-Europos house church with baptistery, destroyed c. 256; reconstructed at Yale.
claims.source: C. H. Kraeling, The Christian Building (1967).

claims.claim: Tertullian advised delaying baptism of children (c. 200); Origen claimed an apostolic custom of infant baptism; council of Carthage under Cyprian (253) said infants need not wait for the eighth day.
claims.source: Tertullian, On Baptism 18; Origen, Commentary on Romans 5.9; Cyprian, Letter 64 (58).

claims.claim: First Anabaptist baptisms Zurich 21 January 1525 (Grebel); Felix Manz drowned 5 January 1527; John Smyth's congregation Amsterdam 1609.
claims.source: C. Arnold Snyder, Anabaptist History and Theology (1995); B. R. White, The English Baptists of the Seventeenth Century (1983).

claims.claim: Cranmer's Prayer Books 1549 and 1552; Prayer Book banned 1645; restored 1662; Cranmer burned at Oxford 1556.
claims.source: D. MacCulloch, Thomas Cranmer (1996); Act of Uniformity 1662.

claims.claim: Cranmer's lectionary read the Old Testament about once a year and the New Testament three times.
claims.source: BCP 1549/1662 preface 'Concerning the Service of the Church' and Calendar.

claims.claim: Prayer Book psalter is Coverdale's (1535 Bible, via the Great Bible).
claims.source: Standard; e.g. Alan Jacobs, The Book of Common Prayer: A Biography (2013).

claims.claim: Lectionary for Mass 1969; Revised Common Lectionary 1992.
claims.source: Ordo Lectionum Missae (1969); Consultation on Common Texts (1992).

claims.claim: Ancient literacy perhaps 10% or less; Christians early adopters of the codex.
claims.source: W. V. Harris, Ancient Literacy (1989); H. Y. Gamble, Books and Readers in the Early Church (1995).

claims.claim: Charles Wesley wrote over 6,000 hymns.
claims.source: Standard; e.g. S. T. Kimbrough (ed.), Charles Wesley: Poet and Theologian (1992).

claims.claim: Corinthian dining-room capacity and rich-poor division at the Lord's Supper.
claims.source: G. Theissen, The Social Setting of Pauline Christianity (1982); J. Murphy-O'Connor, St. Paul's Corinth (2002).

claims.claim: 1662 rubric requires each parishioner to communicate at least three times a year, Easter being one.
claims.source: BCP 1662, rubrics after the Communion.

claims.claim: Catholic canon 844; Church of England Canon B 15A; Wesley's 'converting ordinance' (Journal, 27–28 June 1740).
claims.source: Code of Canon Law (1983) c. 844; Canons of the Church of England B 15A; Wesley, Journal.

claims.claim: Leavened bread in the East, unleavened in the West, a grievance in 1054; Vatican II allows Communion under both kinds; Welch's unfermented grape juice 1869.
claims.source: Sacrosanctum Concilium 55; Council of Trent Session XXI; standard histories of 1054 and of Thomas Welch.

claims.claim: Quakers began in the 1650s around George Fox; Barclay's Apology Latin 1676, English 1678; Barclay imprisoned in Aberdeen.
claims.source: H. Barbour and J. W. Frost, The Quakers (1988); Barclay, Apology, Gutenberg #56487.

claims.claim: Voltaire in England 1726–1728; Letters published in English 1733 before the French (1734).
claims.source: Morley's introduction, Gutenberg #2445; standard biographies.

claims.claim: Hume: superstitious religion pleases with 'frivolous observances'; Kant: 'counterfeit service' (Afterdienst).
claims.source: Hume, Natural History of Religion (1757) XIV; Kant, Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason (1793), Part IV.

claims.claim: Pew (2017): about 27% of US adults 'spiritual but not religious'.
claims.source: Pew Research Center, 6 September 2017.

claims.claim: Attendance more than weekly linked to about a third lower mortality in the Nurses' Health Study.
claims.source: S. Li et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 176 (2016) 777–785; content/library/faith-and-health.md.

claims.claim: Trent: sacraments confer grace ex opere operato to those who place no obstacle.
claims.source: Council of Trent, Session VII (1547), Canons on the Sacraments in General 6–8.

claims.claim: Ambrose acclaimed bishop of Milan in 374 while unbaptised; baptised Augustine 387; On the Mysteries c. 390.
claims.source: Paulinus, Life of Ambrose 6–9; Augustine, Confessions IX.6; NPNF II.10 introduction.

claims.claim: Corbie controversy (Paschasius and Ratramnus, 9th century); Berengar's recantation (1059, 1079); Lateran IV (1215) 'transubstantiated'.
claims.source: Lateran IV, canon 1; Gary Macy, The Theologies of the Eucharist in the Early Scholastic Period (1984).

claims.claim: Aquinas on substance and accidents in the Eucharist.
claims.source: Summa Theologiae III, qq. 75–77.

claims.claim: Luther rejected transubstantiation in The Babylonian Captivity (1520), image of fire in iron; most Lutherans reject 'consubstantiation'.
claims.source: Luther, Babylonian Captivity; Formula of Concord SD VII.

claims.claim: Marburg Colloquy October 1529: agreement on 14 of 15 articles; Luther chalked 'Hoc est corpus meum'; refused Zwingli's hand ('different spirit'); Zwingli killed at Kappel 1531.
claims.source: Marburg Articles; H. Sasse, This Is My Body (1959); MacCulloch, Reformation (2003).

claims.claim: Calvin's spiritual real presence.
claims.source: Calvin, Institutes IV.17 (1559).

claims.claim: Black Rubric added 1552, dropped 1559, restored 1662 with 'corporal' for 'real and essential'.
claims.source: BCP 1552 and 1662, declaration on kneeling.

claims.claim: John Frith burned 1533.
claims.source: Foxe, Acts and Monuments; standard histories.

claims.claim: Ignatius calls the Eucharist 'the flesh of our Saviour'; Tertullian 'figure of his body'; Augustine Sermon 272.
claims.source: Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 7; Tertullian, Against Marcion IV.40; Augustine, Sermon 272.

claims.claim: Leuenberg Agreement 1973; ARCIC Windsor statement 1971.
claims.source: Texts of both agreements.

claims.claim: Zadok, Locus iste (Bruckner 1869, Linz votive chapel), Dear Lord and Father (Whittier 1872), Ubi caritas (Maundy Thursday), Ave verum (Mozart 1791).
claims.source: content/music.json notes.

claims.claim: Wertmüller was working in Philadelphia in 1795.
claims.source: Not in the gallery description; NGA object record / biographies of Adolph-Ulrich Wertmüller (in America 1794–1796).

claims.claim: Jordans Meeting House built 1688, William Penn buried there.
claims.source: Britain Yearly Meeting / Historic England listing.

flags: PLEASE CHECK: this journey overlaps the switched-off Sunday guide (content/sunday.json); session 7's practical advice follows it. Needs a minister's review (Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox, Free Church), and the Quaker material a Friend's review.

PLEASE CHECK the BCP Morning Prayer text: from an Andrews University transcription of a twentieth-century printing (prayers for Queen Elizabeth), not a 1662 printing. Dropped initial letters restored ('ALMIGHTY', 'THE grace'); reference line '2 Corinthians xiii.' removed. Per DECISIONS, short liturgical texts of the BCP are quoted; Crown letters patent noted.

PLEASE CHECK Voltaire's translator: the 1733 English translation is usually credited to John Lockman (d. 1771). The Gutenberg file is Henry Morley's 1894 Cassell edition of that translation and names no translator. Published 1733, and any translator died long before 1955, so it qualifies.

PLEASE CHECK Barclay's edition: Gutenberg #56487 is a later ('eighth') English edition of the 1678 text; capitals and spelling are that edition's. Sidenotes, footnote markers [n] and italic underscores removed.
PLEASE CHECK Luther (Reu, 1915; Reu d. 1943): the Gutenberg text's misprint 'our a hearts' is kept as printed and noted in the context box.

Removed from New Advent texts (Justin, Cyril, Ambrose): inserted Scripture references (e.g. 'John 3:5', 'Luke 22:19', 'Hebrews 2:14-15', 'Matthew 26:26') and stray spaces before punctuation. Didache: site verse numbers and braces removed. ANF bracketed glosses kept.
Cyril's Mystagogical Lectures: authorship (Cyril or his successor John) is said to be debated in the text.
Kant 'counterfeit service' and Hume 'frivolous observances': in our own words with short phrases; check against the translations a reviewer prefers.
'Luther wrote on his desk I am baptised' is given as 'is said to': the tradition is popular rather than well sourced (cf. Large Catechism IV, 'I am baptised'). PLEASE CHECK or cut.
The octagonal-baptistery inscription attributed to Ambrose (for the baptistery of Santa Tecla) is attributed, not certain.
